bibl.title: Adaptive Conversational Agents: Exploring the Effect of Individualized Design on User Experience

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Initial results from our pilot study (n=37) confirm that individualized CA design can enhance the user experience.

span.label: adaptive conversational agent design
span.quote: This research examines the influence of individualized CA design on the user experience.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: To examine the influence of individualized CA design on the user experience and test our hypotheses, we conduct an online experiment applying a within-subject design (Erlebacher, 1977).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Accommodating one's communication style to the interlocutor signals an attitude toward them and thereby steers how the speaker and the interaction are evaluated
span.quote: The theory suggests that humans adapt their communication style to show their attitude toward the interlocutor and steer the evaluation of the speaker and the interaction (Giles et al., 2010).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An interaction partner that accommodates the user's needs signals attention and caring, which raises perceived social presence, which in turn produces enjoyment
span.quote: When a (human or technology) interaction partner considers the needs and preferences of the interlocutor during the interaction, this signals attention and caring (Bitner et al., 1990; Giles et al., 2010), thereby enhancing the perceived social presence (Hess et al., 2009; Van Pinxteren et al., 2020).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Matching the chatbot's communication style to the user's cognitive abilities lowers the cognitive effort the interaction demands and raises its efficiency, which drives re-use intention
span.quote: For example, if the CA’s communication style matches the user's cognitive abilities, this will likely decrease the required cognitive effort and improve interaction efficiency (Giles et al., 2010; Goodhue and Thompson, 1995).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The unequal split between rational and intuitive participants left that group underpowered, producing the absence of significant differences
span.quote: A possible explanation could be the imbalance of the number of participants that were classified as rational or intuitive (10 compared to 4)—which will be addressed in the main study.

span.label: The pilot's sample was small and the authors treat the whole design as provisional pending a larger main study.
span.quote: Despite its limited sample size, our pilot study offers valuable insights into the effect of individualized CAs on the user experience:

span.label: The within-subjects design may bias later user-experience responses; a between-subjects design is being considered instead.
span.quote: First, it is worth considering a between-subjects design instead of a within-subjects design, as this prevents participants from being biased in their responses to the user experience questionnaire by previous questions.

span.label: The cognitive-style group was imbalanced (10 rational vs 4 intuitive), which may explain the absence of significant effects there.
span.quote: A possible explanation could be the imbalance of the number of participants that were classified as rational or intuitive (10 compared to 4)—which will be addressed in the main study.

span.label: Only two user characteristics were studied, and separately; other characteristics and their combinations remain unexamined.
span.quote: Furthermore, we have considered two user characteristics (separately) so far, but there are more worth investigating (e.g., other cognitive styles).

span.label: The summarised benefit does not carry the exceptions the results report: in one group the adapted agent was no better on satisfaction, and the UN-adapted agent was rated higher on enjoyment.
span.quote: The user experience with the individualized CA was rated better in both experimental groups, with two exceptions—in the rational/intuitive cognitive style group, service satisfaction did not differ for the individualized and the not adapted CA and enjoyment was rated better for the not adapted CA.

span.label: The design used may bias the responses it collects, and the authors say a different design would prevent it.
span.quote: First, it is worth considering a between-subjects design instead of a within-subjects design, as this prevents participants from being biased in their responses to the user experience questionnaire by previous questions.

span.label: Two user characteristics were examined, separately, and the authors state the interplay between them was not investigated.
span.quote: Furthermore, we have considered two user characteristics (separately) so far, but there are more worth investigating (e.g., other cognitive styles). Likewise, the interplay of combinations of different user characteristics as well as the influence of different CA design characteristics on the user experience might be interesting to explore.

span.label: The constructs are measured entirely by item sets borrowed from other studies, so the measurement inherits whatever those instruments assume.
span.quote: To measure the variables, we adopted established measures from prior literature. Users’ characteristics ‘need for interaction’ and ‘rational/intuitive cognitive style’ are measured using four items based on Dabholkar (1996) and ten items based on Hamilton et al. (2016).

span.label: the theory of how humans accommodate their speech to an interlocutor, re-applied to design a chatbot that accommodates its style to the user
span.quote: Our study will further contribute to research by adapting communication accommodation theory (Giles et al., 2010) to the context of human-AI interaction, thereby showing that adapting the CA’s communication style to users has the potential to positively influence their user experience.

span.label: user experience - operationalised as three separate measured constructs: service satisfaction as the evaluative attribute, enjoyment as the hedonic one, re-use intention as the pragmatic one
span.quote: To evaluate the user experience, we draw on the overall evaluation of the interaction (i.e., service satisfaction), as well as hedonic (i.e., enjoyment) and pragmatic (i.e., re-use intention) attributes

span.label: satisfaction - a construct the paper notes is used for two different things across disciplines: user attitudes ABOUT A SYSTEM, or the perception of SERVICE INTERACTIONS
span.quote: Satisfaction is a central construct of interest in IS and other disciplines (e.g., marketing, service science) (Deng et al., 2010), used to measure user attitudes about a system (Melone, 1990) or the perception of service interactions (Oliver, 1980).

span.label: builds-on → communication accommodation theory (Giles et al., 2010)
span.quote: Drawing on communication accommodation theory (Giles et al., 2010), we derive a research model, that is tested in an online experiment.

span.label: extends → Altmeyer et al. (2020); Danckwerts et al. (2019); Gnewuch et al. (2020)
span.quote: However, the majority of prior studies on the individualization of CAs or AI-based systems has two crucial shortcomings: First, they do not explicitly adapt the system design to user characteristics (e.g., Altmeyer et al., 2020; Danckwerts et al., 2019; Gnewuch et al., 2020), yet only measure perceived individualization (i.e., instead of actively presenting different levels of individualization of the CA, they only ask users in how far they think the given system was adapted to them).

span.label: user experience —operationalised-as→ service satisfaction
span.quote: To evaluate the user experience, we draw on the overall evaluation of the interaction (i.e., service satisfaction), as well as hedonic (i.e., enjoyment) and pragmatic (i.e., re-use intention) attributes

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Therefore, we conducted t-tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests, as not all our measures were normally distributed.

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Therefore, we conducted t-tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests, as not all our measures were normally distributed.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: The analysis results show that in the experimental group “need for interaction” both enjoyment (V = 72.5, p < .05) and re-use intention (V = 74, p < .05) were significantly higher for the individualized CA.

span.label: median split
span.quote: Based on the questionnaire responses, we determined the threshold levels for the user characteristics using a median split, as has been done by prior studies (e.g., Lee et al., 2010; Wang and Benbasat, 2013).

span.label: power analysis
span.quote: An a priori power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) with a significance level of 0.05 determined a minimum sample size of 90 participants to achieve a statistical power of 0.95 for detecting a medium effect size (d = 0.5).

span.label: effect size (Cohen's d)
span.quote: An a priori power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) with a significance level of 0.05 determined a minimum sample size of 90 participants to achieve a statistical power of 0.95 for detecting a medium effect size (d = 0.5).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Using this classification in the subsequent pilot study, eight (out of 16) participants were categorized as having a high need for interaction (group mean = 4.56, SD = 1.27)

span.label: In the need-for-interaction group, both enjoyment and re-use intention were significantly higher for the chatbot adapted to the user than for the non-adapted chatbot.
span.quote: The analysis results show that in the experimental group “need for interaction” both enjoyment (V = 72.5, p < .05) and re-use intention (V = 74, p < .05) were significantly higher for the individualized CA.

span.label: In the rational/intuitive cognitive-style group, none of the user-experience differences between the adapted and non-adapted chatbot reached statistical significance.
span.quote: In addition, for the experimental group “rational/intuitive cognitive style”, no evidence for statistically significant differences in the user experience could be demonstrated.

span.label: The improvement in service satisfaction from individualization was not statistically significant.
span.quote: For service satisfaction (V = 57, p = .22) the observed improvement was not statistically significant.

span.label: Individualization improved ratings in both groups except that, for cognitive-style adaptation, service satisfaction was unchanged and enjoyment was actually rated higher for the non-adapted chatbot.
span.quote: The user experience with the individualized CA was rated better in both experimental groups, with two exceptions—in the rational/intuitive cognitive style group, service satisfaction did not differ for the individualized and the not adapted CA and enjoyment was rated better for the not adapted CA.

span.label: Enjoyment of the chatbot adapted to the user's need for interaction averaged 5.70 against 4.90 for the one-size-fits-all chatbot.
span.quote: Whereas the enjoyment with the CA that was adapted to users’ need for interaction was rated substantially better (mean = 5.70 compared to mean = 4.90)

span.label: conversational agents (CAs)
span.quote: Conversational agents (CAs) are AI-based systems that interact with users in natural language, thereby offering a natural and intuitive user interface (Kock, 2004; McTear et al., 2016).

span.label: cognitive style
span.quote: Psychology describes and measures cognitive abilities with cognitive styles, defined as “consistencies in an individual’s manner of cognitive functioning, particularly with respect to acquiring and processing information” (Kozhevnikov, 2007, p. 464).

span.label: intuitive cognitive style
span.quote: An intuitive cognitive style is characterized by the reliance on first impressions and gut feelings and a contextualized and automatic decision-making process (Hamilton et al., 2016).

span.label: rational cognitive style
span.quote: By contrast, a rational cognitive style is characterized by a deliberate and analytical decision-making process (Epstein et al., 1996; Hamilton et al., 2016).

span.label: need for interaction
span.quote: The user characteristic ‘need for interaction’ captures users’ fundamental desire to retain personal contact with others (Dabholkar, 1996).

span.label: user characteristics
span.quote: Defined as users’ fundamental dispositions and traits (Al-Natour and Benbasat, 2009; Zhang et al., 2009), individual user characteristics are stable over time and across task contexts (Kozhevnikov, 2007; Thatcher and Perrewé, 2002).

span.label: enjoyment
span.quote: Enjoyment refers to “the extent to which the activity of interacting […] is perceived to be enjoyable in its own right” (Qiu and Benbasat, 2009, p. 154).

span.label: CA design adaptation (individualized vs. not adapted chatbot)
span.term: CA design adaptation (individualized vs. not adapted chatbot)
span.quote: In the experiment, participants interact with both a not adapted chatbot as instantiation of a text-based CA and an individualized chatbot.

span.label: which user characteristic the CA is adapted to (need for interaction vs. rational/intuitive cognitive style)
span.term: which user characteristic the CA is adapted to (need for interaction vs. rational/intuitive cognitive style)
span.quote: Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups, i.e., either the adaptation to the user characteristic need for interaction, or the adaptation to users’ rational or intuitive cognitive style.

span.label: user experience: service satisfaction, perceived enjoyment, re-use intention
span.term: user experience: service satisfaction, perceived enjoyment, re-use intention
span.quote: To evaluate the user experience, we measure service satisfaction based on three items adopted from Verhagen et al. (2014), perceived enjoyment based on five items adopted from Qui and Benbasat (2009), as well as re-use intention based on three items adapted from Bhattacherjee (2001).

span.label: post-interaction user-experience questionnaire administered after each chatbot
span.term: post-interaction user-experience questionnaire administered after each chatbot
span.quote: Next, participants interact with a not adapted CA and fill out a questionnaire measuring their user experience (i.e., their service satisfaction, perceived enjoyment, and re-use intention).

span.label: experimental task (pizza ordering, identical across conditions)
span.term: experimental task (pizza ordering, identical across conditions)
span.quote: As an experimental task for the CA interaction, we chose pizza ordering, which is a typical service task for which companies often implement CAs (e.g., Domino’s Pizza) (McTear, 2017; Thomaz et al., 2020).

span.label: 37 — participants recruited for the pilot study
span.quote: To examine the influence of individualization of CAs on the user experience, we conducted a pilot study with 37 participants (16 female, average age = 27 years, range 18-56

span.label: 30 — usable data sets analysed after excluding inattentive participants
span.quote: Thus, we analyzed 30 data sets (16 in the group “need for interaction”, 14 in the group “rational/intuitive cognitive style”) to derive initial results.

span.label: seven — data sets dropped for failing attention checks
span.quote: To ensure high-quality data, we excluded seven data sets due to inattention (i.e., when they failed attention check questions).

span.label: 52 — participants in the pre-study used to set the classification thresholds
span.quote: we conducted a pre-study with 52 participants (18 female, average age = 25 years, range 18-55).

span.label: 4.7 — threshold score on the 7-point scale above which a participant counts as having a high need for interaction
span.quote: Our pre-study revealed that participants scoring on average 4.7 or higher on the 7-point need for interaction scale (Dabholkar, 1996) can be classified as having a high need for interaction

span.label: mean = 5.70 compared to mean = 4.90 — enjoyment rating of the CA adapted to need for interaction versus the one-size-fits-all CA
span.quote: Whereas the enjoyment with the CA that was adapted to users’ need for interaction was rated substantially better (mean = 5.70 compared to mean = 4.90)

span.label: 90 — minimum sample size the power analysis requires for the planned main study
span.quote: An a priori power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) with a significance level of 0.05 determined a minimum sample size of 90 participants to achieve a statistical power of 0.95 for detecting a medium effect size (d = 0.5).

span.label: n = 8 — participants in the two qualitative pre-tests validating the chatbots
span.quote: All CAs were validated in two qualitative pre-tests (n = 8).

span.label: 10 compared to 4 — imbalance between participants classified as rational and as intuitive, offered as the reason for the null result in that group
span.quote: A possible explanation could be the imbalance of the number of participants that were classified as rational or intuitive (10 compared to 4)—which will be addressed in the main study.
